Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
One type of indirect proof is the so-called proof by contradiction.

Content:
The method of proof by contradiction is based on the fact that a statement [MATH: P] is logically equivalent to the implication
[MATH: \lnot P \Rightarrow \mathbf{c},]
where [MATH: \mathbf{c}] is a contradiction.

Content:
To see why this is equivalent to [MATH: P,] note that since [MATH: A\Rightarrow B\equiv \lnot A\lor B,] we have
[MATH: ¬P⇒c|≡¬(¬P)∨c; ≡P∨c; ≡P.]

Content:
So, instead of directly proving a statement [MATH: P,] we can assume that [MATH: \lnot P] is true and show that this leads to a contradiction.

Content:
The outline of a typical proof by contradiction is as follows:

Content:
> Statement. [MATH: P]
>
> Proof.
>
> > We'll prove that [MATH: \lnot P] leads to a contradiction.
> >
> > Assumption: Suppose [MATH: \lnot P.]
> >
> > Explanation of what [MATH: \lnot P] means using axioms, definitions, or other results.
> >
> > Algebraic techniques, logic, and further definitions or axioms are used to demonstrate a contradiction through a series of inferences.
> >
> > Conclusion: So, we got a contradiction, which means our assumption [MATH: \lnot P] is false. Therefore, [MATH: P] is true.

Content:
In many cases, proving that the negation of a statement leads to a contradiction is easier than proving the original statement. In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove various statements using the contradiction.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Proving a Statement by Contradiction

Content:
Let's prove the following proposition by contradiction:

Content:
> [MATH: 10x+4y \neq 1] for all [MATH: x,y \in \mathbb{Z}.]

Content:
First, let's write down the formal statement [MATH: P] that we wish to prove:

Content:
[MATH: \phantom{\lnot}P: \quad \forall x, y\in\mathbb Z,\, 10x+4y \neq 1]

Content:
To prove that [MATH: P] is true, we assume that [MATH: \lnot P] is true and show this leads to a contradiction.

Content:
[MATH: \lnot P: \quad \exists x, y\in\mathbb Z,\, 10x+4y = 1]

Content:
We begin our proof as follows:

Content:
> Assume, for a contradiction, that there exists [MATH: x,y \in \mathbb{Z}] such that [MATH: 10x+4y = 1.]

Content:
The idea is to divide both sides by a specific number and show that the left-hand side is an integer while the right-hand side is not.

Content:
Since [MATH: 10] and [MATH: 4] have a common factor of [MATH: 2,] we can divide the left-hand side by this factor without introducing fractional coefficients.

Content:
> Dividing both sides by [MATH: 2] gives
> [MATH: 10x + 4y|= 1; (10x + 4y)/(2)|= (1)/(2); (10x)/(2) + (4y)/(2)|= (1)/(2); 5x + 2y|= (1)/(2).]

Content:
Finally, we show that we've reached a contradiction.

Content:
> Since [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] are integers, we have that [MATH: 5x+2y] is an integer.
>
> But this is a contradiction since [MATH: \dfrac12] is not an integer.

Content:
Since we have a contradiction, our assumption that [MATH: \lnot P] is true is incorrect. Hence, [MATH: P] is true, and we write our conclusion as follows:

Content:
> Therefore, [MATH: 10x+4y \neq 1] for any [MATH: x,y \in \mathbb{Z}.]

Content:
